text: To capitulate is to stop resisting and accept the other side's terms. It is stronger than simply agreeing — the word comes from military surrender, so it describes someone who held out as long as they could and finally ran out of room. After winning nearly every smoker's lawsuit for decades, the tobacco firms were not persuaded that their critics were right; they lost the ground they had been defending, and the 1998 settlement is what that collapse looked like.

Obfuscation is deliberately making something hard to understand — clouding a subject so people cannot see it clearly. It is a slipperier charge than lying, because an obfuscator need not say anything false, only pile up doubt and distraction until the plain fact is lost in the fog. That is precisely what Boulder accuses the oil firms of: not denying their own scientists, but muddying the picture for so long that the public never saw it sharply enough to demand action.

To recuse yourself is to step aside from a decision because you have a personal stake in the outcome. In law the test is not whether you would actually be swayed, but whether a reasonable onlooker could doubt that you were neutral — so a judge who owns shares in one of the companies involved withdraws rather than just promising to be fair. Because the Supreme Court has nine justices, Alito stepping out leaves eight to decide Boulder's appeal.

In law, damages is a plural noun meaning money a court orders one side to pay the other for harm done — not the harm itself. So winning damages from oil firms means getting them to hand over cash, which is a different goal from forcing them to stop selling fuel. Watch the grammar: the damage was severe, but the damages were $200bn.

A suit here is short for lawsuit — a formal claim one party files against another in court — and has nothing to do with clothing. The article shortens it both ways, so the old 1990s tobacco suits and the Big Oil lawsuits are the same kind of thing. Someone who files one is said to sue.

Litigation is the whole business of fighting disputes out in court — the process, not any single case. Calling the opioid cases opioid litigation treats dozens of separate lawsuits as one long campaign, which is exactly the point Justice Kagan is making about tobacco, opioids and now oil. A lawyer who does this work is a litigator.

A reckoning is the moment when someone is finally made to answer for what they have done, after a long stretch of getting away with it. The word's older sense is arithmetic — settling up an account — and that sense of a bill coming due is still inside it. Asking whether a similar reckoning is coming for oil companies means asking whether their turn to pay has arrived.

To allege something is to claim it formally without having yet proved it. Journalists lean on this word constantly, and for a precise reason: writing that the city alleges the companies concealed the dangers reports the accusation accurately while taking no position on whether it is true. If a court agrees in the end, the allegation becomes a finding.

To conceal something is to hide it on purpose, keeping it out of sight so others cannot find it. The deliberateness is the whole weight of the word in this story — spending decades concealing the dangers of fossil fuels is an accusation of choice, not of oversight, and that is what Boulder has to prove.

To commission a piece of work is to order it and pay for it — a report, a painting, a study. It is a sense worth catching, since the same word also means granting someone an officer's rank in the military. Here it matters who paid: the 1968 report was commissioned by the oil industry's own trade group, so the warning about carbon dioxide came from inside the industry, not from its critics.

Ambient means surrounding you on all sides — the ambient temperature of a room, or ambient noise you cannot locate. The lawyer uses it to make a legal point out of a physical fact: because air and water are ambient, they do not stay inside state borders, so one state's courts cannot sensibly set the rules for them.

An enclave is a small territory entirely enclosed by another one — a patch of land surrounded by a country that is not its own. Justice Barrett borrows the map word for the law: pollution is an enclave of federal common law, meaning a fenced-off area where only federal rules operate, however much territory the states hold around it.

Unprecedented means never done before, with no earlier case to point to. In court that is close to an insult, because judges lean heavily on precedent — what previous courts decided in similar situations. Calling Boulder's suit an unprecedented use of state law is a way of saying it has no footing in anything a court has already approved.

When a court has held something, it has officially decided it, and that ruling now binds later cases. This is a specialised sense of hold worth learning early, since every court story uses it — the Supreme Court has held that federal law governs interstate pollution claims is reporting settled law, not an opinion anyone is still arguing about. The noun is a holding.

Shares are slices of ownership in a company; owning some makes you a part-owner who profits when the company does well. That is why owning shares in oil companies is a problem for a judge hearing a case against oil companies — a ruling in their favour would make his own holding more valuable. The American word for the same thing is stock.

To light up, said of a smoker, is simply to light a cigarette and start smoking. The phrase carries the tobacco companies' entire old defence in three words: no one forced them to light up means the choice belonged to the smoker, so the harm was their own doing. That argument won them nearly every case for decades.

To carve out something is to create a deliberate exception inside a general rule, as though cutting a piece away from a larger block. It is standard legal and business usage — a contract carves out one product from a ban. Justice Barrett carved out more room for state efforts, meaning she wanted the federal rule to leave the states some space rather than swallowing everything.

To get around a problem is to find a way past an obstacle you cannot remove — going round it rather than through it. The article uses it for a clever legal manoeuvre: smoking looked like a matter of individual choice, so states got around that by suing over the public costs of treating smokers instead of over any one smoker's decision.

Owing to means because of, in a slightly formal register — you will meet it constantly in serious writing. It introduces the cause of whatever follows, so owing to the ambient nature of air and water sets up the reason the lawyer then gives for why federal law has to govern.

For something to stand in the way is to block progress toward a goal, like an obstacle planted in a path. Saying legal obstacles stand in the way of winning damages is a signal about the rest of the article: the problem is not whether the harm is real, but whether the law allows this particular lawsuit to work.

Big Tobacco is the nickname for the handful of giant cigarette manufacturers, treated as a single bloc because they so often acted as one. The Big-something formula gets reused for any industry seen as powerful and hard to hold to account — Big Oil, Big Pharma, Big Tech — and the whole argument of this article is that the first of them set the pattern for suing the next.

Big Oil means the major oil and gas companies taken together as a political force — firms like Exxon Mobil and Suncor. The label borrows its shape from Big Tobacco on purpose, which is the comparison the headline is built on, though the article is careful about one real difference: oil is broadly useful in a way cigarettes never were.

The Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States, and the last stop for a case — nine justices, appointed for life, who choose the small number of appeals they will hear. What it decides becomes the law for the whole country, which is why a single Boulder lawsuit reaching it matters far beyond Colorado.

In everyday speech a nuisance is a minor annoyance; in law it is a specific kind of claim about unreasonable interference with the use of property — the neighbour whose bonfire smoke fills your house every evening. Public nuisance extends that to things everyone uses and nobody privately owns, like air or a river, which is why a city rather than an injured resident is doing the suing. The lawyer's crack about being sued for refilling his car is aimed at the obvious weak spot: if fouling shared air counts, every driver does a little of it.

Oral argument is the hearing where each side's lawyer stands before the justices and answers their questions out loud, after both have already filed written briefs. It is usually brief — often an hour — and it is the one public, unscripted part of a Supreme Court case. The questions judges ask there are the main clue outsiders get about which way they are leaning, which is why the article reads so much into Kavanaugh's and Barrett's remarks.

Federal law is law made for the whole country, as against the law each individual state writes for itself; when the two genuinely conflict, the federal one wins and the state rule is pushed aside. Common law is the part built up from judges' past decisions rather than written by a legislature. So federal common law governing interstate pollution means the courts themselves have decided that this subject belongs at the national level — which would leave Boulder's state-law case with nothing to stand on.

Fossil fuels are coal, oil and natural gas — fuels made from the remains of organisms buried for hundreds of millions of years. Burning them releases the carbon those organisms stored, as carbon dioxide, which is the link between selling fuel and changing the climate that this whole lawsuit depends on.

Carbon dioxide, written CO2, is the gas produced whenever carbon-based fuel is burned. It lets sunlight through but absorbs heat radiating back up from the ground, so more of it in the air means more heat kept near the surface. The 1968 report's warning about increased levels of carbon dioxide is the scientific core of Boulder's claim that the industry knew early.

The American Petroleum Institute is the oil and gas industry's main trade association in the United States — an industry group, meaning an organisation funded by companies in a business to do research and lobby on their behalf. Its role here is what makes the 1968 report so damaging to the companies: the warning was commissioned by the industry's own body, so it is evidence of what the firms themselves were told.

Exxon Mobil is the largest American oil company, and one of the two defendants Boulder is suing. It appears twice in the story for different reasons: as a company being sued, and as the employer of the scientists who in the late 1970s found that burning fossil fuels could have dramatic environmental effects.

Suncor Energy is a Canadian oil company and Boulder's other defendant; it runs a refinery in Colorado. The article notes that its predecessor company — the earlier firm it grew out of — had links to the American Petroleum Institute in 1968, which is how a 58-year-old report becomes relevant to a lawsuit against Suncor today.

Boulder is a city of about 100,000 people in Colorado, sitting at the foot of the Rocky Mountains. It is the plaintiff here — the side bringing the lawsuit — and it is suing over floods, extreme heat and wildfires, all hazards that have grown worse in the American West.

Samuel Alito is one of the Supreme Court's nine justices and among its most conservative, appointed in 2006. He does not appear in this case at all, which is the point of mentioning him: because he owns shares in oil companies, he recused himself, leaving eight justices to decide.

Elena Kagan, appointed in 2010, is one of the court's three liberal justices. Her remark that the case appears to be based on the old 1990s tobacco suits is read in the article as sympathy for Boulder, since she is describing the lawsuit as following a model that already worked twice.

Brett Kavanaugh is a conservative justice appointed in 2018 who often sits near the court's middle on close questions. His line that this kind of pollution is a federal-law matter unless Congress speaks otherwise is the clearest signal in the article against Boulder, because it would place the dispute outside the reach of Colorado's own law.

Amy Coney Barrett, appointed in 2020, is a conservative justice who has sometimes broken from the other conservatives in close cases. The article places her between the two positions: she wanted to leave the states more room than Kavanaugh would, but still agreed that pollution sits in a federal enclave.

Kannon Shanmugam is the lawyer arguing for the oil companies — one of the small group of specialists who appear at the Supreme Court again and again. Every argument on the companies' side in this article is his: that the suit tries to resolve political questions in court, that it is an unprecedented use of state law, and that its logic would reach as far as a driver refilling a car.

Opioids are powerful painkillers made from or modelled on opium, including prescription drugs like OxyContin. Heavy prescribing in America produced mass addiction, and states and cities sued the drugmakers and distributors over the public cost of it, winning tens of billions in settlements. That is the chapter two Kagan has in mind: the same model as tobacco, run a second time.

A collective-action problem is one where everybody would gain if everybody acted, but no single player gains enough by acting alone to make it worth doing — so nobody moves. Climate change is the standard example, since one country cutting emissions bears the whole cost while the benefit spreads worldwide. It is the article's closing point, and the sharpest difference from smoking: a smoker who quits gets the full benefit of quitting.
